# Summary {#summary}

This is the first DigiKat annual review. It describes what the Croatian digital space published on
Catholic themes during {{scalar:report_year}}, how much of it there is, who publishes it, what it is
about and in what tone.

The database covers the Croatian digital media space as a whole, from websites and social networks
to video and comments. It contains {{scalar:corpus_rows}} posts collected {{scalar:corpus_span}}.
The {{scalar:report_year}} calendar year accounts for {{scalar:total_posts}} posts.

{{fragment:summary}}

Every number in this review is computed from the database and can be reproduced. None was entered
by hand.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Two recurring terms

A *post* is one database record: an article, social-media post, video or comment. A *source* is the
media outlet or account from which a post came, not an individual person.
:::

{{fragment:block_fig01_ten_numbers}}

# Ecosystem map {#ecosystem}

## How large is the space? {#scale}

In {{scalar:report_year}} we recorded {{scalar:total_posts}} posts on Catholic themes. More than
half, {{scalar:web_share}}, appeared on the web, on websites and portals rather than social media.
Facebook accounts for {{scalar:facebook_share}} and YouTube for {{scalar:youtube_share}}.

{{fragment:block_fig02_platforms}}

{{fragment:table_platform}}

Post count and reach are not the same. Facebook accounts for roughly a quarter of posts but
{{scalar:facebook_reach_share}} of recorded reach. The web publishes more; networks reach wider.

{{fragment:block_fig03_months}}

## Who leads? {#actors}

Posts come from {{scalar:distinct_sources}} distinct sources. The space is highly dispersed, but
that dispersion can mislead: the top ten sources account for {{scalar:top10_share}} of the year,
while {{scalar:sources_to_half}} sources produce half of annual volume. The rest is a long tail in
which thousands of sources publish only a few times a year.

{{fragment:block_fig09_concentration}}

{{fragment:table_league}}

The {{scalar:league_outlets}} leading institutional media outlets together carry
{{scalar:league_share}} of the year.

Among sources whose editorial identity has been reviewed, confessional media account for
{{scalar:confessional_share_classified}} of posts. The rest comes from secular and local media.

{{fragment:table_typology}}

The groups in this table describe the relationship between interactions and reach. Some actors have
a broad audience that seldom reacts; others have a smaller community that responds to almost every
post.

## Where is the conversation moving? {#movement}

In the second half of the year, the web published {{scalar:web_stream_change}} more than in the
second half of {{scalar:baseline_year}}. The number of tracked web sources changed by
{{scalar:web_stream_sources_change}} over the same period, so the increase does not come from wider
tracking. Facebook grew by {{scalar:facebook_stream_change}}, but its number of tracked pages also
rose by {{scalar:facebook_stream_sources_change}}.

{{fragment:block_fig08_stream}}

{{fragment:table_stream}}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Questions raised by the data

- Is the web growing because the same sources publish more, or because new titles are appearing?
- Does Facebook growth accompany audience growth, or only growth in the number of tracked pages?
- How often does the same source publish the same material across several platforms?
:::

# Thematic currents {#themes}

## What did the space discuss? {#theme-profile}

The year is led by what the Church does every week. Spirituality and liturgy—Mass, feast days,
sacraments and prayer—is the leading theme in {{scalar:lead_theme_docs}} of posts and accounts for
{{scalar:lead_theme_mentions}} of all theme mentions. Church governance and structure follows,
then bioethical and cultural themes.

{{fragment:block_fig05_themes}}

{{fragment:table_themes}}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Myth and data

**Myth.** Media coverage of the Church appears mainly when a scandal or conflict breaks out.

**Data.** Abuse and the crisis of trust account for {{scalar:abuse_share}} of all theme mentions;
internal Church disputes account for {{scalar:disputes_share}}. The four days that depart most from
the year's ordinary rhythm are liturgical or papal.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Questions raised by the data

- Which themes grow when a feast day does not carry them?
- Do the same sources cover bioethics and liturgy?
- How long does one theme hold the space before another replaces it?
:::

# Atmosphere of the discourse {#tone}

## What language is used? {#tonality}

The year sounds more positive than one might expect. Predominantly positive vocabulary appears in
{{scalar:tone_positive_share}} of posts, while the annual mean is {{scalar:tone_mean}} on a scale
from −1 to +1. The subject itself explains much of this: notices about Mass, blessings and
celebrations contain positive words.

{{fragment:block_fig06_tone_themes}}

{{fragment:table_tone}}

Alongside tone, we track conflict vocabulary: terms connected with anger, fear, attack, division
and scandal. The annual mean is {{scalar:cli_mean}} such words per thousand words.

The difference between confessional and secular sources is visible and measurable. Confessional
sources carry {{scalar:cli_confessional}} conflict words per thousand, while secular sources carry
{{scalar:cli_secular}}, or {{scalar:cli_ratio}} as many. Secular media are more likely to cover the
Church when the subject is a dispute; confessional sources also cover the community's ordinary life.

{{fragment:block_fig07_tone_labels}}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Questions raised by the data

- Does the vocabulary gap remain when posts about the same event on the same day are compared?
- How does tone change within an event arc, from the first report to later commentary?
- Do national and local media differ in tone as much as confessional and secular media do?
:::

# Event focus {#events}

## What marked the year? {#moment}

The year has one clear peak. On {{scalar:peak_day}} we recorded {{scalar:peak_posts}} posts. That is
{{scalar:peak_z}} standard deviations above the average collected day and the largest count of the
year. The complete {{scalar:peak_arc_span}} arc carries {{scalar:peak_arc_posts}} posts.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Moment of the year: the death and funeral of Pope Francis

Pope Francis died on 21 April {{scalar:report_year}}, Easter Monday, and his funeral took place on
26 April. Both dates are among the days that diverge most sharply from the annual rhythm. “Popes and
the Vatican” reaches its annual maximum, accompanied by spirituality and liturgy and by Church
governance.
:::

{{fragment:block_fig04_year}}

{{fragment:table_events}}

The other three peaks are the Assumption of Mary, Christmas Day and the second papal date. No annual
peak emerged from a controversy.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Questions raised by the data

- Who reported the Pope's death first, and who relayed the news?
- For how many days does an event hold attention after its peak?
- Does a major event leave a trace in volume months later?
:::

# Special chapter: Catholic social teaching and the economy {#special}

Each edition contains one completed study separate from the recurring indicators. This year's study
asks which parts of Catholic social teaching enter digital public discussion of the economy.

The study searched {{scalar:special_linked}} posts in which religious and economic language meet,
then manually checked a sample. Doctrinal terms such as the dignity of work, the preferential option
for the poor, subsidiarity and the common good appear in {{scalar:special_headline}} of those
encounters.

{{fragment:table_special}}

The study concludes that the Church speaks rarely in economic debate, but when it does, its language
is relatively consistent with its own vocabulary.

# What comes next {#gaps}

This is the first edition; each future edition will add one layer.

**Composite annual index.** A single number summarising the year and its direction. It will be
introduced once the reference year is frozen, so the baseline does not change with what it measures.

**Change arrows.** From the next edition, each ranking will show change from the previous year, and a
separate section will return to previously published numbers.

**Transmission of the Church voice.** When a secular outlet covers a subject already discussed by a
Church source, how often and how quickly does the Church framing appear?

**Audience.** How people encounter these materials, how much they trust them and what they do with
them. This requires a dedicated survey, sample and instrument.

{{fragment:table_indicators}}

# Methodology {#methodology}

**Database.** {{scalar:corpus_rows}} posts, {{scalar:corpus_span}}. One inclusion rule applies across
the entire period. At least one of {{scalar:corpus_terms}} religious terms must occur within the
first three thousand characters, and a second-pass model must score the post above
{{scalar:corpus_threshold}}. Manually read samples estimate precision at about
{{scalar:corpus_precision}}.

**Scope.** The database is theme-based rather than source-based. It includes confessional and
secular sources whenever a post discusses Catholic themes, as well as regional material including
content from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

**Year.** The year contains {{scalar:total_posts}} posts across {{scalar:collected_days}} collected
days. The {{scalar:gap_span}} interruption is marked in every relevant display and excluded from all
averages. The median day around the interruption carried {{scalar:median_day}} posts, so the gap is
estimated to omit about {{scalar:gap_estimated_posts}} posts.

**Comparisons.** Collection changed in the middle of {{scalar:baseline_year}}. Every comparison in
this review is therefore made within the same collection stream and over an equal number of days.

**Peaks.** A day is flagged when it lies at least three standard deviations above the annual mean.
The threshold was fixed before data inspection, and the mean and dispersion use collected days only.
Days separated by at most two days belong to one arc. A peak in the data identifies a date, not a
cause, so the thematic composition of every named day was checked.

**Themes.** A frozen dictionary of sixteen categories is applied to a random sample of
{{scalar:theme_docs}} posts, or {{scalar:theme_rate}} of the corpus year. Share of mentions divides
all dictionary matches, so one post may contribute to several themes; leading theme assigns one
category to each post. The dictionary recognises words, not meaning.

**Tone.** The tone score uses Croatian sentiment dictionaries applied to lemmas, on a −1 to +1 scale,
for a sample of {{scalar:tone_docs}} posts, or {{scalar:tone_rate}} of the corpus year. Conflict words
count terms of anger, fear, disgust and conflict per thousand words. Both measures describe a post's
vocabulary, not the author's position or the truth of a claim.

**Source labels.** Editorial labels for confessional and secular sources have proposal status and
cover {{scalar:classified_coverage}} of annual volume, so comparisons by label are indicative.

**Naming.** Only institutional media with at least five posts during the year may be named.
Individual accounts are never named, and cells below the threshold are suppressed.

**Reproducibility.** `INDICATORS.md` contains the complete definition of each indicator, its
comparability rule and change history. Reviewed aggregates are published with the report.
